claim: Sea urchin larvae possess a muscular apparatus that surrounds their esophagus and produces contractile force.
source: Sea urchin larvae possess a muscular apparatus that surrounds their esophagus and produces contractile force (Burke, 1981; Burke and Alvarez, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burke, 1981 and Burke and Alvarez, 1988.

claim: Sea urchin muscle cells originate from mesoderm.
source: These muscle cells originate from mesoderm and adapt the myogenic fate by segregating from the other three non-skeletogenic mesodermal (NSM) lineages at the early gastrula stage (Ruffins and Ettensohn, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruffins and Ettensohn, 1996.

claim: Sea urchin myoblasts segregate from other non-skeletogenic mesodermal lineages at the early gastrula stage.
source: These muscle cells originate from mesoderm and adapt the myogenic fate by segregating from the other three non-skeletogenic mesodermal (NSM) lineages at the early gastrula stage (Ruffins and Ettensohn, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruffins and Ettensohn, 1996.

claim: The first appearance of myoblasts is seen at the late gastrula stage as a few cells in the oral vegetal domain of each coelomic sac at the tip of the archenteron.
source: The first appearance of myoblasts is seen at the late gastrula stage as a few cells in the oral vegetal domain of each coelomic sac at the tip of the archenteron and they express a number of muscle-specific transcription regulators (Andrikou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Andrikou et al., 2013.

claim: At the prism stage, myoblasts extend pseudopods towards the midline of the esophagus, increase in number and diameter, fuse to each other, and form the circumesophagael contractile bands.
source: Few hours later, at the prism stage, these cells extend pseudopods towards the midline of the esophagus, increase in number and diameter, fuse to each other, and finally form the circumesophagael contractile bands (Burke and Alvarez, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burke and Alvarez, 1988.

claim: FGFR1 is expressed in all FoxC-positive cells at the very early gastrula stage.
source: At the very early gastrula stage, FGFR1 was expressed in all FoxC-positive cells (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by double fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At the late gastrula stage, only a number of FGFR1 transcripts overlap with FoxC-positive cells at the tip of the archenteron.
source: whilst at the late gastrula stage (48 hr), only a number of FGFR1 transcripts overlap with FoxC-positive cells at the tip of the archenteron (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by co-expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: FGFA transcripts are observed in the ventrolateral ectodermal regions in the vicinity of FoxC-positive cells at the very early gastrula stage.
source: Moreover, FGFA transcripts were observed in the ventrolateral ectodermal regions in the vicinity of FoxC-positive cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by double fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 70% of pluteus larvae treated with SU5402 from 26 hr showed an abnormal elongated archenteron missing the pyloric and possibly the anal sphincter constrictions.
source: 70% of the 300 pluteus larvae treated with SU5402 from 26 hr showed an abnormal elongated archenteron missing the pyloric and possibly the anal sphincter constrictions, although the cardiac sphincter was still formed (Figure 2A–D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from SU5402 treatment shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: All SU5402-treated larvae had shorter spicules and their triradiate skeleton was never fully shaped.
source: Moreover, all larvae had shorter spicules and their triradiate skeleton was never fully shaped possibly due to the inhibition of FGFR2, which is specifically expressed in the skeletogenic primary mesenchyme cells (PMCs) that produce the larval skeleton (Rottinger et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and citation to Rottinger et al., 2008.

claim: In SU5402-treated larvae, the coelomic pouches were not formed and the circumesophagael muscle fibers were completely absent.
source: Finally, the coelomic pouches were not formed and the circumesophagael muscle fibers were completely absent when tested for MHC gene expression by FISH at the prism stage (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by FISH data for MHC gene expression shown in Figure 2D.

claim: U0126 treatment greatly reduced MHC protein level in treated larvae.
source: Again, the level of MHC protein was greatly reduced in the treated larvae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: FGF signaling through MAPK/ERK pathway is involved in muscle development.
source: These findings show an involvement of FGF signaling through MAPK/ERK pathway in muscle development.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of SU5402 and U0126 treatments showing reduced muscle formation.

claim: In 90% of FGFR1 morphant larvae, a malformation of coelomic pouches and a severe down-regulation of the MHC protein level were evident.
source: Although in 90% of the morphant larvae, a malformation of coelomic pouches (Figure 2F) and a severe down-regulation of the MHC protein level were evident (Figure 2G,H)
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 2F, G, H.

claim: 70% of FGFR1 morphant larvae displayed a fully elongated gut with the cardiac and anal sphincters well formed.
source: 70% of the larvae displayed a fully elongated gut, with the cardiac and anal sphincters well formed (Figure 2F)
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In 30% of FGFR1 morphant larvae, both cardiac and anal sphincters were absent or partly formed.
source: while in the rest cases both sphincters were absent or partly formed (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: FGFR1 morphants showed an abnormal extension of cilia in the apical ectoderm.
source: In addition, an abnormal extension of cilia in the apical ectoderm was observed (Figure 2H insert) that provides a putative additional role of FGFR1 in patterning the apical organ (Paola Oliveri, personal communication)
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 2H insert.

claim: FGFR1 morphants showed a reduction of cilia in the gut lumen.
source: An evident reduction of the cilia in the gut lumen is also observed (Figure 2H)
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: FGFR1 is not involved in PMC patterning and subsequent skeleton formation.
source: Moreover, the larval skeleton and the formation of pigment cells were not affected, confirming that FGFR1 is not involved either in PMC patterning and subsequent skeleton formation or in pigment cell development (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data showing no effect on skeleton shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FGFR1 is not involved in pigment cell development.
source: Moreover, the larval skeleton and the formation of pigment cells were not affected, confirming that FGFR1 is not involved either in PMC patterning and subsequent skeleton formation or in pigment cell development (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data showing no effect on pigment cells shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In 60% of FGFR1 dominant negative injected embryos, the cardiac and anal sphincters were absent.
source: An even more severe phenotype was obtained by injecting the embryos with the mRNA encoding FGFR1 Dn with the cardiac and anal sphincters being absent in 60% of the cases (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by dominant negative RNA injection data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: FoxY expression did not change when FGF signaling was perturbed.
source: While FoxY expression did not change when FGF signaling was perturbed (Figure 3A–D)
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: A severe impact was observed in FoxC and FoxF transcript levels in all FGF signaling-perturbed embryos.
source: a severe impact was observed in FoxC and FoxF transcript levels in all treated embryos (Figure 3E–L).
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3E-L.

claim: Ese expression was unaffected by FGFR1 perturbation.
source: To check whether the specification of other oral NSM cell lineages were affected as well by the FGFR1 perturbation, we also tested the expression of Ese, a marker of the blastocoelar cell lineage, and found it unaffected (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: FoxC and FoxF factors act downstream of FGF signaling.
source: These results further support the involvement of FGF signaling in myogenesis and demonstrate that FoxC and FoxF factors are acting downstream of it.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FoxC and FoxF expression is reduced when FGF signaling is perturbed.

claim: Ets1/2 expression showed a clear co-localization with FoxC transcripts at around 30 hr.
source: On the other hand, Ets1/2 expression showed a clear co-localization with FoxC transcripts at around 30 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E,F) that perfectly corresponds to the onset of myogenesis, suggesting a putative role of Ets1/2 as one of the terminal effectors of MAPK pathway acting during myoblast specification.
evidence: Supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E,F.

claim: In 90% of FoxY morphants, the archenteron was fully elongated with signs of incomplete differentiation and the coelomic pouches were lacking.
source: In 90% of the FoxY morphants, the archenteron was fully elongated with signs of incomplete differentiation and the coelomic pouches were lacking, as was shown previously (Song and Wessel, 2012; Materna et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data and citations to Song and Wessel, 2012 and Materna et al., 2013.

claim: In FoxY morphants, the MHC level was severely reduced.
source: The MHC level was also severely reduced (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: 80% of FoxC morphants showed a fully invaginated and partially compartmentalized archenteron, missing completely the coelomic pouches and MHC protein.
source: 80% of the FoxC morphants showed a similar morphological alteration; the archenteron was fully invaginated and partially compartmentalized, missing completely the coelomic pouches and MHC protein (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In 90% of FoxF morphant larvae, a fully tripartite archenteron was present with disorganized coelomic pouches and a great decrease in the MHC level.
source: In 90% of the FoxF morphant larvae, a fully tripartite archenteron was present with disorganized coelomic pouches and a great decrease in the MHC level (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 95% of FoxL1 MO-injected larvae possessed a differentiated archenteron with disrupted coelomic pouches and reduced MHC protein level.
source: 95% of the FoxL1 MO-injected larvae possessed a differentiated archenteron with disrupted coelomic pouches and reduced MHC protein level (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 85% of MyoD2 morphants showed an elongated archenteron, and in most cases with reduced sphincter constrictions.
source: 85% of the MyoD2 morphants showed an elongated archenteron, and in most of the cases with reduced sphincter constrictions.
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data.

claim: In MyoD2 morphants, the coelomic pouches were not formed properly and the MHC level was dramatically reduced.
source: The coelomic pouches were also not formed properly and the MHC level was dramatically reduced (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In 80% of Six1/2 morphants, the archenteron was elongated but not differentiated, the coelomic pouches were absent, and the MHC level was decreased.
source: In 80% of the Six1/2 morphants, the archenteron was elongated but not differentiated, the coelomic pouches were absent, and the MHC level was decreased (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Embryos injected with the MO targeted to the late Six1/2 isoform were fully pigmented.
source: Interestingly, unlike what previously shown by using an MO against the early isoform of Six1/2, which negatively affects pigmentation (Ransick and Davidson, 2012), embryos injected with the MO targeted to the late Six1/2 isoform were fully pigmented (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D and citation to Ransick and Davidson, 2012.

claim: 95% of Tbx6 morphants had a milder phenotype, with no signs of malformed coelomic pouches and only a partial disrupted muscle fiber assembly.
source: Finally, 95% of Tbx6 morphants had a milder phenotype, with no signs of malformed coelomic pouches and only a partial disrupted muscle fiber assembly as shown by MHC immunostaining (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: FoxY positively regulates itself at the early gastrula stage.
source: At the early gastrula stage, FoxY and FoxC expression was strongly reduced in FoxY MO-injected embryos (Figure 5A–D), suggesting that FoxY positively regulates itself and FoxC.
evidence: Supported by FISH data in FoxY morphants shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: FoxY positively regulates FoxC at the early gastrula stage.
source: At the early gastrula stage, FoxY and FoxC expression was strongly reduced in FoxY MO-injected embryos (Figure 5A–D), suggesting that FoxY positively regulates itself and FoxC.
evidence: Supported by FISH data in FoxY morphants shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: FoxY positively regulates FoxF and FoxL1 at the mid and late gastrula stages.
source: This positive regulation continued to the mid and late gastrula stages and FoxY also positive regulated the other two Fox factors, FoxF and FoxL1 (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by NanoString and qPCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Nanos expression was downregulated in FoxY morphants.
source: The expression of Nanos, a germ cell marker (Juliano et al., 2006) that is part of the molecular signature of the myoblasts precursors at that developmental time point (Andrikou et al., 2013), was also downregulated in FoxY morphants (Figure 5E,F and Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by FISH and quantitative data in FoxY morphants shown in Figure 5E,F and Figure 6, and citations to Juliano et al., 2006 and Andrikou et al., 2013.

claim: FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 are downstream of FoxC at the mid gastrula stage.
source: FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 were downstream of FoxC at the mid gastrula stage.
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis results.

claim: FoxC negatively regulates itself at the mid gastrula stage.
source: Expression of FoxF and FoxL1 required FoxC input, whereas FoxC negatively regulated itself (Figure 5G,H and Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by FISH and quantitative data in FoxC morphants shown in Figure 5G,H and Figure 6.

claim: FoxF and FoxL1 expression required FoxC input at the mid gastrula stage.
source: Expression of FoxF and FoxL1 required FoxC input, whereas FoxC negatively regulated itself (Figure 5G,H and Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by FISH and quantitative data in FoxC morphants shown in Figure 5G,H and Figure 6.

claim: FoxY expression domain was expanded in the FoxF morphants to include the oral vegetal region of the archenteron tip at the late gastrula stage.
source: At the late gastrula stage, FoxY expression domain was expanded in the FoxF morphants to include the oral vegetal region of the archenteron tip, where myogenesis takes place (Figure 5I,J).
evidence: Supported by FISH data in FoxF morphants shown in Figure 5I,J.

claim: At the mid gastrula stage, FoxY positively regulates Pitx2, MyoR, Six1/2, and ScratchX.
source: In addition to the inter-regulatory properties of the Fox factors, at the mid gastrula stage, FoxY also positively regulated Pitx2 (Hibino et al., 2006), MyoR, a gene expressed in sea urchin mesoderm but not in the myoblasts (Andrikou et al., 2013), Six1/2 and ScratchX.
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis results and citations to Hibino et al., 2006 and Andrikou et al., 2013.

claim: FoxC activates Tbx6 at the mid gastrula stage.
source: FoxC also activated Tbx6 and repressed Not and Dachshund (Dachs), an aboral NSM gene in the sea urchin embryo (Luo and Su, 2012).
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis results and citation to Luo and Su, 2012.

claim: FoxC represses Not and Dachshund at the mid gastrula stage.
source: FoxC also activated Tbx6 and repressed Not and Dachshund (Dachs), an aboral NSM gene in the sea urchin embryo (Luo and Su, 2012).
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis results and citation to Luo and Su, 2012.

claim: Six1/2 activates FoxL1, MyoR, and Pitx2 at the mid gastrula stage.
source: Six1/2 appeared to activate FoxL1, MyoR, and Pitx2, as previously suggested (Hibino et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis results and citation to Hibino et al., 2006.

claim: At the late gastrula stage, FoxY activates SoxE gene.
source: At the late gastrula stage, FoxY continued to activate the aforementioned downstream factors although its effect on Six1/2 was diminished and activated in addition SoxE gene.
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis results.

claim: FoxL1 gives positive inputs to FoxF, MyoR, ScratchX, and Pitx2 at the late gastrula stage.
source: FoxL1 gave positive inputs to FoxF, MyoR, ScratchX, and Pitx2 and repressed Dachs, FoxY, and Not.
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis results.

claim: FoxL1 represses Dachs, FoxY, and Not at the late gastrula stage.
source: FoxL1 gave positive inputs to FoxF, MyoR, ScratchX, and Pitx2 and repressed Dachs, FoxY, and Not.
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis results.

claim: Tbx6 represses FoxY, Dach, and Scl at the late gastrula stage.
source: Tbx6 repressed FoxY, Dach, and Scl and activated Pitx2 and MyoR.
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis results.

claim: Tbx6 activates Pitx2 and MyoR at the late gastrula stage.
source: Tbx6 repressed FoxY, Dach, and Scl and activated Pitx2 and MyoR.
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis results.

claim: FGF signaling is necessary for specifying naive NSM cells to myoblast precursors at the very early gastrula stage.
source: We show that FGF signaling is necessary for specifying naive NSM cells to myoblast precursors at the very early gastrula stage.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from FGF signaling perturbation experiments.

claim: Four Fox family factors FoxY, FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 constitute the central part of the myogenic GRN model.
source: The four Fox family factors FoxY, FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 (Tu et al., 2006) constitute the central part of our myogenic GRN model and are activated sequentially.
evidence: Supported by perturbation analysis and citation to Tu et al., 2006.

claim: FoxY, FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 are activated sequentially.
source: The four Fox family factors FoxY, FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 (Tu et al., 2006) constitute the central part of our myogenic GRN model and are activated sequentially.
evidence: Supported by temporal expression analysis and perturbation data.

claim: The muscle progenitors originate from a pool of unspecified cells located at the oral/lateral periphery of the vegetal plate at the mesenchyme blastula stage.
source: In this study, we propose that the muscle progenitors originate from a pool of unspecified cells located at the oral/lateral periphery of the vegetal plate at the mesenchyme blastula stage and they adapt the myogenic fate by receiving an inductive signal at the moment of gastrulation.
evidence: Proposed based on expression pattern analysis and perturbation data.

claim: Muscle progenitors adapt the myogenic fate by receiving an inductive signal at the moment of gastrulation.
source: In this study, we propose that the muscle progenitors originate from a pool of unspecified cells located at the oral/lateral periphery of the vegetal plate at the mesenchyme blastula stage and they adapt the myogenic fate by receiving an inductive signal at the moment of gastrulation.
evidence: Proposed based on FGF signaling perturbation data.

claim: All developmental decisions regarding the separation of all four NSM regulatory states take place during the interval between the blastula and the very early gastrula stage.
source: This would further imply that all developmental decisions regarding the separation of all four NSM regulatory states (pigment, blastocoelar, muscle, and coelomic pouch cells) take place during the interval between the blastula and the very early gastrula stage.
evidence: Inferred from the timing of FGF signaling requirement and cell fate specification.

claim: FGF-signaling cascade triggers the emergence and/or promotes the expansion of muscle lineage progenitors in different organisms.
source: FGF-signaling cascade is reported to trigger the emergence and/or promote the expansion of muscle lineage progenitors in different organisms and probably possessed an ancestral role in mesoderm patterning (at least in deuterostomes), along with other developmental processes.
evidence: Supported by knowledge from literature on FGF signaling in various organisms.

claim: FGF signaling probably possessed an ancestral role in mesoderm patterning in deuterostomes.
source: FGF-signaling cascade is reported to trigger the emergence and/or promote the expansion of muscle lineage progenitors in different organisms and probably possessed an ancestral role in mesoderm patterning (at least in deuterostomes), along with other developmental processes.
evidence: Speculated based on comparative analysis across deuterostomes.

claim: Genes encoding FGF and FGFR were already present in the last common ancestor of all metazoans.
source: Genes encoding FGF and FGFR were already present in the last common ancestor of all metazoans, but the origin of the FGF/FGFR couple appears to be an innovation specific to the Eumetazoa, potentially linked to the increase of animal complexity (Bertrand et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bertrand et al., 2014.

claim: The origin of the FGF/FGFR couple appears to be an innovation specific to the Eumetazoa.
source: Genes encoding FGF and FGFR were already present in the last common ancestor of all metazoans, but the origin of the FGF/FGFR couple appears to be an innovation specific to the Eumetazoa, potentially linked to the increase of animal complexity (Bertrand et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bertrand et al., 2014.

claim: The FGF/FGFR couple is potentially linked to the increase of animal complexity.
source: Genes encoding FGF and FGFR were already present in the last common ancestor of all metazoans, but the origin of the FGF/FGFR couple appears to be an innovation specific to the Eumetazoa, potentially linked to the increase of animal complexity (Bertrand et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bertrand et al., 2014.

claim: FoxY is a direct target of the Delta/Notch signal.
source: As shown elsewhere, FoxY is a direct target of the D/N signal, produced in the adjacent NSM.
evidence: Supported by knowledge from literature.

claim: The positive autoregulation of FoxY maintains its own expression during gastrulation.
source: Therefore, the positive autoregulation of FoxY maintains its own expression during gastrulation when cells invaginate into the blastocoel and may be away from the signaling source.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FoxY positively regulates itself and the need to maintain expression during cell movement.

claim: FoxC initially needs both positive inputs from FGF signaling and FoxY to be activated.
source: FoxC initially needs both positive inputs from FGF signaling and FoxY to be activated but then acts as an autorepressor in order to stabilize its number of transcripts.
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis showing FoxC requires both FGF and FoxY.

claim: FoxC acts as an autorepressor to stabilize its number of transcripts.
source: FoxC initially needs both positive inputs from FGF signaling and FoxY to be activated but then acts as an autorepressor in order to stabilize its number of transcripts.
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis showing FoxC negatively regulates itself.

claim: Tbx6 cooperates redundantly with other factors in an OR logic.
source: Tbx6 seems to cooperate redundantly with other factors in an OR logic (Davidson, 2010), which also explains the mild phenotype seen in the Tbx6 perturbations.
evidence: Inferred from the mild phenotype observed in Tbx6 morphants and citation to Davidson, 2010.

claim: MyoD activates the differentiation gene battery set composed of structural genes such as MHC.
source: The differentiation drivers, such as MyoD (Andrikou et al., 2013), are seen in the bottom of the GRN and probably activate the differentiation gene battery set, composed of a number of structural genes (e.g., MHC) that account for the specific function of the muscle cell.
evidence: Inferred from the hierarchical position of MyoD in the GRN and citation to Andrikou et al., 2013.

claim: FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL subfamilies are clustered in most metazoan genomes.
source: Among them, FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL subfamilies are of particular interest because they are clustered in most metazoan genomes and usually involved in mesoderm specification/differentiation processes (Mazet et al., 2006; Shimeld et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mazet et al., 2006 and Shimeld et al., 2010.

claim: FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL subfamilies are usually involved in mesoderm specification/differentiation processes.
source: Among them, FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL subfamilies are of particular interest because they are clustered in most metazoan genomes and usually involved in mesoderm specification/differentiation processes (Mazet et al., 2006; Shimeld et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mazet et al., 2006 and Shimeld et al., 2010.

claim: In vertebrates, FoxC specifies the dorsal mesoderm and derivatives.
source: Moreover, a linked activation or an overlapping expression has been reported in some cases, as in vertebrates, where FoxC specifies the dorsal mesoderm and derivatives, while FoxF patterns the lateral mesoderm and derivatives (Beh et al., 2007; Zinzen et al., 2009; Amin et al., 2010; Fritzenwanker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beh et al., 2007; Zinzen et al., 2009; Amin et al., 2010; Fritzenwanker et al., 2014.

claim: In vertebrates, FoxF patterns the lateral mesoderm and derivatives.
source: Moreover, a linked activation or an overlapping expression has been reported in some cases, as in vertebrates, where FoxC specifies the dorsal mesoderm and derivatives, while FoxF patterns the lateral mesoderm and derivatives (Beh et al., 2007; Zinzen et al., 2009; Amin et al., 2010; Fritzenwanker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beh et al., 2007; Zinzen et al., 2009; Amin et al., 2010; Fritzenwanker et al., 2014.

claim: In the sea urchin, a cluster of FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 genes is present.
source: In the sea urchin, where a cluster of FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 genes is present (Andrikou et al., 2013), we witness a similar regulatory logic where the different Fox factors pattern in an overlapping fashion in different compartments of the coelomic pouches.
evidence: Supported by citation to Andrikou et al., 2013.

claim: In the sea urchin, different Fox factors pattern in an overlapping fashion in different compartments of the coelomic pouches.
source: In the sea urchin, where a cluster of FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 genes is present (Andrikou et al., 2013), we witness a similar regulatory logic where the different Fox factors pattern in an overlapping fashion in different compartments of the coelomic pouches.
evidence: Supported by expression pattern analysis and citation to Andrikou et al., 2013.

claim: The FoxC, FoxF, FoxL1 cluster was probably expressed initially in developing mesodermal tissues.
source: This cluster was probably expressed initially in developing mesodermal tissues and further evolved in regulating the specification and compartmentalization of mesodermal derivatives.
evidence: Speculated based on comparative analysis and expression patterns.

claim: FoxC is the first of the three genes FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 to be turned on in the myogenic lineage.
source: The expression patterns and sequential activation of FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 genes in time reflect the linkage properties of the retained cluster: among the three genes, FoxC is the first to be turned on in the myogenic lineage and is necessary for the activation of the downstream factors FoxF and FoxL1, which are inter-regulated.
evidence: Supported by temporal expression analysis and perturbation data.

claim: FoxC is necessary for the activation of the downstream factors FoxF and FoxL1.
source: The expression patterns and sequential activation of FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 genes in time reflect the linkage properties of the retained cluster: among the three genes, FoxC is the first to be turned on in the myogenic lineage and is necessary for the activation of the downstream factors FoxF and FoxL1, which are inter-regulated.
evidence: Supported by perturbation analysis showing FoxC is required for FoxF and FoxL1 expression.

claim: FoxF and FoxL1 are inter-regulated.
source: The expression patterns and sequential activation of FoxC, FoxF, and FoxL1 genes in time reflect the linkage properties of the retained cluster: among the three genes, FoxC is the first to be turned on in the myogenic lineage and is necessary for the activation of the downstream factors FoxF and FoxL1, which are inter-regulated.
evidence: Inferred from perturbation analysis.

claim: By 24 hr post fertilization, the separation of the different NSM regulatory states is defined.
source: By 24 hr post fertilization, the separation of the different NSM regulatory states is defined.
evidence: Supported by expression pattern analysis of NSM markers.

claim: At 9 hr post fertilization, Delta ligand produced by the skeletogenic mesoderm activates a Delta/Notch cascade.
source: At 9 hr post fertilization, Delta ligand produced by the skeletogenic mesoderm activates a D/N cascade, which subsequently initiates Gcm and GataE transcription in all NSM cells (Ransick and Davidson, 2006; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ransick and Davidson, 2006 and Lee et al., 2007.

claim: Delta/Notch cascade initiates Gcm and GataE transcription in all NSM cells.
source: At 9 hr post fertilization, Delta ligand produced by the skeletogenic mesoderm activates a D/N cascade, which subsequently initiates Gcm and GataE transcription in all NSM cells (Ransick and Davidson, 2006; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ransick and Davidson, 2006 and Lee et al., 2007.

claim: At 24 hr, the NSM GRN becomes regionalized into distinct oral and aboral NSM GRNs in consequence of Nodal signaling.
source: Later, at 24 hr, the NSM GRN becomes regionalized into distinct oral and aboral NSM GRNs in consequence of Nodal signaling through the immediate expression of a Nodal target, Not, in the oral NSM.
evidence: Supported by knowledge from literature on Nodal signaling.

claim: Nodal signaling causes the repression of the aboral GRN in the oral NSM cells.
source: This causes the repression of the aboral GRN in the oral NSM cells, and the aboral NSM cells still express Gcm and GataE as part of the regulatory state of the pigment cell lineage (Materna et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Materna et al., 2013.

claim: The myogenic GRN structure has diverged extensively among animal groups.
source: Despite the conserved regulatory modules found in the system, the myogenic GRN structure has diverged extensively among animal groups.
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis of myogenic GRNs across different animal groups.

claim: The level of functional importance of homologous transcriptional regulators is often diversified among animal groups.
source: As a consequence, the level of the functional importance of the homologous transcriptional regulators (e.g., Six1/2 in sea urchin and Ceh-34 in C. elegans or MyoD in vertebrates and Nautilus in Drosophila) (this study, [Olson and Klein, 1994; Balagopalan et al., 2001; Amin et al., 2009]), as reflected from the position within the GRN, is often diversified.
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis and citations to Olson and Klein, 1994; Balagopalan et al., 2001; Amin et al., 2009.

claim: New, lineage-specific genes are recruited in myogenic GRNs.
source: New, lineage-specific genes are recruited (FoxY in sea urchin), and 'master regulatory genes' either have been lost completely (e.g., the absence of Pax3/7 ortholog in the sea urchin) or lose their hierarchical position within the network (e.g., Nautilus in Drosophila and MyoD in vertebrates)
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis showing FoxY is sea urchin-specific and absence of Pax3/7 in sea urchin.

claim: The same transcription factor families are used repeatedly in myogenic contexts across different animal systems.
source: However, the fact that the same factors are used over and over again in such different animal systems indicates that the modular components are somehow required for keeping their myogenic activity during evolutionary time.
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis showing conservation of transcription factor families.

claim: The ancestral myogenic function may have been preserved in a more distant family member rather than the homologous gene.
source: It seems that as transcription factor families expanded and functionally diversified during evolution, the ancestral myogenic function may have been preserved in a more distant family member, rather than the homologous gene, providing the system with several regulatory alternatives, and explaining the high degree of evolutionary plasticity of developmental GRN architecture (Andrikou and Arnone, 2015).
evidence: Speculated based on comparative analysis and citation to Andrikou and Arnone, 2015.
